questions.stem: A test harness runs on 4 operating systems, 3 browsers and 5 screen sizes, choosing exactly one of each. How many distinct configurations are there?
questions.explanation: The three choices are made independently and jointly define one configuration, so the **product rule** applies: $4 \times 3 \times 5 = 60$. Use the product rule when a single outcome requires a choice from *each* category, and the sum rule only when the outcome comes from exactly one of several disjoint categories.

distractorRationale.a: Multiplies only the first two factors, omitting screen size
distractorRationale.c: Adds instead of multiplying $(4 + 3 + 5 = 12)$ and then doubles, or applies the sum rule where the choices are not alternatives
distractorRationale.d: Computes $5!$, which would count orderings of five distinct items rather than independent selections

questions.stem: In how many ways can a project group of 3 students be chosen from a class of 10, when the order of selection does not matter? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: Order is irrelevant, so this is a combination: $\binom{10}{3} = \frac{10!}{3!\,7!} = \frac{10 \times 9 \times 8}{3 \times 2 \times 1} = 120$. The division by $3!$ is what removes the duplicate counting of the same three students in different selection orders — without it the answer would be the permutation count 720.

questions.stem: From 10 students, a chairperson, a secretary and a treasurer must be appointed, all posts going to different people. How many ways are there?
questions.explanation: The three posts are distinguishable, so order matters and this is a permutation: $P(10,3) = \frac{10!}{7!} = 10 \times 9 \times 8 = 720$. Equivalently, choose the three people in $\binom{10}{3} = 120$ ways and then assign the posts among them in $3! = 6$ ways, giving $120 \times 6 = 720$.

distractorRationale.a: 120 is $\binom{10}{3}$, the count when the three roles are interchangeable
distractorRationale.c: $10^3$ allows the same person to hold more than one post, which the question forbids

questions.stem: How many distinct bit strings of length 8 exist?
questions.explanation: Each of the 8 positions independently takes one of 2 values, so by the product rule the count is $2^8 = 256$. This is the same computation as the size of the power set of an 8-element set, since a bit string of length 8 *is* a subset indicator — and it is why a byte holds 256 distinct values.

distractorRationale.b: $2^6$ or $8^2$; neither matches 8 positions with 2 choices each
distractorRationale.d: $8! = 40320$ counts orderings of 8 distinguishable items, but the bits are not distinguishable objects being arranged

questions.stem: Of 60 students, 35 take Data Structures, 28 take Discrete Mathematics and 12 take both. How many take neither? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: By inclusion–exclusion, the number taking at least one course is $|D \cup M| = 35 + 28 - 12 = 51$. The 12 must be subtracted because adding the two totals counts them twice. Those taking neither are $60 - 51 = 9$. Notice that $35 + 28 = 63$ exceeds the class size, which by itself proves the overlap must be non-empty.

questions.stem: A committee of 3 must be chosen from 6 men and 4 women, and must include at least one woman. How many committees are possible?
questions.explanation: Count by complement, which is far cleaner than summing the cases of one, two and three women. All committees: $\binom{10}{3} = 120$. Committees violating the constraint are the all-male ones: $\binom{6}{3} = 20$. So the answer is $120 - 20 = 100$. Checking directly confirms it: $\binom{4}{1}\binom{6}{2} + \binom{4}{2}\binom{6}{1} + \binom{4}{3} = 4(15) + 6(6) + 4 = 100$.

distractorRationale.b: Counts every committee, ignoring the at-least-one-woman constraint
distractorRationale.c: Subtracts $\binom{6}{3}$ twice, or subtracts the all-female committees as well
distractorRationale.d: Reports $\binom{6}{3}$, the number of committees that were *excluded*

questions.stem: A tutorial group has 25 students. What does the generalised pigeonhole principle guarantee about the days of the week on which their birthdays fall?

options.text: Some day of the week is the birthday of at least 4 of them
Some day of the week is the birthday of at least 3 of them, but 4 cannot be guaranteed
Every day of the week is the birthday of at least 3 of them
Nothing can be guaranteed without knowing the actual birthdays

questions.explanation: Placing $n$ objects into $m$ boxes forces some box to hold at least $\lceil n/m \rceil$ objects. Here $\lceil 25/7 \rceil = \lceil 3.57 \rceil = 4$. The bound is tight: if only 3 fell on each day the total would be at most $21 < 25$, so a fourth is unavoidable — while a distribution of 4, 4, 4, 4, 3, 3, 3 shows that no stronger claim holds.

distractorRationale.b: Under-applies the ceiling; 3 per day accounts for only 21 students, leaving 4 unplaced
distractorRationale.c: The principle guarantees a claim about *some* box, never about every box — six days could have three each
distractorRationale.d: The conclusion is purely counting-based and holds for every possible assignment of birthdays

questions.stem: A hash function mapping 1000 distinct keys into 500 buckets must produce at least one collision, regardless of how well it is designed.
questions.explanation: True, by the pigeonhole principle: 1000 keys into 500 buckets forces some bucket to receive at least $\lceil 1000/500 \rceil = 2$ keys. No hash function, however sophisticated, can be injective when the domain is larger than the codomain. This is why a hash table is defined by its collision-resolution strategy rather than by any attempt to avoid collisions — and why a *perfect* hash function requires the key set to be known in advance and at most as large as the table.

questions.stem: A password is exactly 4 characters long, each drawn from the 26 lowercase letters, with repetition allowed. How many passwords are possible, and which rule applies?

options.text: $26^4$, by the product rule with repetition allowed

questions.explanation: Each of the 4 positions is filled independently from all 26 letters, because repetition is allowed, so the product rule gives $26^4 = 456{,}976$. The distinguishing question is always whether choices are independent: permutations arise when each selection removes an option, and combinations when order is irrelevant. Neither applies here.

distractorRationale.a: $P(26,4)$ assumes no letter may repeat, which contradicts the statement
distractorRationale.c: A combination would treat "abcd" and "dcba" as the same password, and would also forbid repetition
distractorRationale.d: The sum rule applies to mutually exclusive alternatives, not to a sequence of independent choices
